3.text: arise on the ground of mutual taunting.

4.text: One tale relates how Head-Nodder, Eᵋleˊnnut, and Aiñaˊɪrg̣ɪn, set off

6.text: “On the way they visited the Aivaˊʟaᵋt.¹ They were living on the shore of a lake. The lake

7.text: was large, and the ice on it quite thick. One water-hole was cut in the middle of the lake. ‘Go

8.text: and fetch some water!’ said Head-Nodder to the younger people. Some went for water. Across

9.text: the water-hole stands Taˊve with wide-spread legs, the big man, the strong one. “What do you

10.text: want?’ — ‘We want water.’ — ‘You shall not have it.’ — They went back. ‘Why have you not

11.text: brought water?’ cries Eᵋleˊnnut. ‘Taˊve did not let us! Now go yourself.’ — ‘I will go!’ cries

12.text: Aiñaˊɪrg̣ɪn. He took the kettle and descended from the shore. Then he came to the water-hole.

13.text: ‘Go away!’ — ‘You shall not have it!’ He came quite close, put the kettle on the ice, caught

14.text: Taˊve and turned him head over heels. He broke with his head the thin ice over the water-hole,

15.text: then he hurled him down on the ground. After that he filled his kettle and went back. ‘Oh, oh!’

16.text: The Easterners seized their spears. ‘Stop that!’ cries Head-Nodder. ‘What strife is this, since we

17.text: are of one tribe? Better let us go and try our anger on some other tribe.’ Then peace was made

18.text: among the people, and all of them set forth against the Taˊn˙ñɪt.”

19.text: During the scuffle at the Anui fair in the year 1895, which I mentioned

20.text: before, Eiˊheli, “the highest chief of the Chukchee,” happened to pick a quarrel

21.text: with the people of the Chaun country. A man from Chaun was killed there.

22.text: Eiˊheli, who was drunk at the time of the scuffle, as usual, saw the corpse,

23.text: and said aloud, “Oh, a man from Chaun! A dog dies a dog’s death!” He

24.text: even pushed the corpse with the toe of his boot. All this became known to

25.text: the Chaun people, and they wanted to make Eiˊheli rue his words. So the

26.text: next morning they met him on his way to the Russian fort, and wanted to

27.text: seize his reindeer. He succeeded in getting loose from them. Then they

28.text: declared that they would kill Eiˊheli just as the Russians had killed one of

29.text: their number. Eiˊheli felt uneasy, and the next morning left, and made for

30.text: his own country. I was then with him. The first five days we travelled quite

31.text: fast, from fear of pursuit. Three years before, Eiˊheli and his people had

32.text: had a quarrel with the people from Chaun, and had nearly come to blows.

33.text: Minor quarrels sometimes arise in connection with conflicting claims to the

34.text: best reindeer-pastures. The tale of “The Happy Suitor” contains a curious

36.text: “Two sons of the hero came back from the reindeer-pasture. The elder said to the father,

37.text: ‘A man of the neighboring camp is pasturing his reindeer on our grounds.’ The father said, ‘Why

38.text: is he angry at us, that he acts in such a manner? This is our fall pasture. Is there not room

39.text: enough farther on? What has angered him?’ Then he said, ‘Take that, and stick it into the

40.text: ground there.’ He gave them a large arrow with a wooden head. ‘With this I want to recover

41.text: my pasture. This is the sign of interdiction of use.’ They went to the pasture and put the arrow

42.text: there. In the fall they drove their herd towards that pasture. Then they could not find the arrow.

43.text: The other man had taken it away, and the pasture was quite trampled down. At last they found

44.text: an old fireplace, and there a remnant of the arrow, all charred. The man had used it to boil some

45.text: soup for himself, so large was the arrow. Some time after that, they pitched their tents in a new
